title: The book that Booker missed
gist: Book review arguing that Emma Cline's novel Switzy, about a wealthy Alzheimer's-afflicted American executive travelling to a Swiss assisted-dying clinic, deserved a place on the Booker Prize shortlist; the critic also previews the shortlist and backs M John Harrison's The End of Everything to win.

themes.theme: Switzy's omission from the Booker shortlist

insights.claim: Emma Cline's Switzy, one of 13 books longlisted for the Booker Prize in July, was widely tipped but left off the shortlist.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Prize snubs can still drive sales via critical controversy.

insights.claim: Actor David Morrissey and Times critic Johanna Thomas-Corr both publicly backed Switzy, Morrissey calling its omission from the shortlist beyond him.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Celebrity and critic endorsement sustain a book's commercial momentum despite the snub.
insights.quote: How it didn’t make the Booker shortlist is beyond me.

insights.claim: The critic judges Elizabeth Strout's shortlisted The Things We Never Say, about a 57-year-old history teacher contemplating suicide in Trump's America, a worthy potential winner.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Assisted death and suicide are prominent themes in current literary fiction.

insights.claim: Switzy's main weakness is a subplot about an old school friend, whose recovered memory critic Chris Power described as too convenient.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Mixed critical reception may partly explain the shortlist omission.
insights.quote: The memory is conveniently unavailable, provoking suspense, and then, just as conveniently, it returns to provide satisfaction.

insights.claim: Switzy depicts end-of-life planning by the 0.1 per cent, with private jets, luxury hotels and chauffeurs framing assisted suicide as a corporate transaction.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Fiction reflects cultural salience of assisted-dying debates and wealth's role in access to it.
insights.quote: this is end-of-life planning by the 0.1 per cent, assisted suicide as corporate transaction
insights.locator: The narrative opens on a February

insights.claim: The novel is unusually granular about assisted-death logistics, including the requirement that a patient remain lucid enough to sign, meaning dementia patients risk sudden disqualification.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Highlights a real policy tension in assisted-dying regimes for dementia patients.
insights.quote: you had to be crazy to do this but not so crazy
insights.locator: She is granular about the logistics

insights.claim: The critic argues the protagonist's wealth is levelling rather than alienating because not even extreme fortune guarantees good fortune when it counts.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.quote: not even an extreme fortune can guarantee good fortune when it really counts

insights.claim: The critic is rooting for M John Harrison's The End of Everything, a speculative tale of societal collapse, to win the Booker Prize announced on Monday.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Booker winners see significant sales uplifts for publishers.
insights.locator: As for this year’s Booker Prize?

insights.claim: The shortlist includes former Booker winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James, comic novelist Luke Kennard's Black Bag, and debut novelist Rebecca Perry's May We Feed the King.
insights.speaker: Susie Mesure
insights.so_what: Shortlist composition for anyone tracking publishing outcomes.
insights.locator: It is up against the toughest
